title: AI Model Deployment
shortDefinition: The process of putting a trained AI model into production where it can serve real predictions.
definition: AI model deployment is the process of taking a trained machine learning model and putting it into a production environment where it can receive real-world input and generate predictions or outputs that your application or business process actually uses. A model that performs well in a data scientist's notebook isn't useful until it's deployed — accessible, reliable, and integrated into the systems and workflows that need its output.

sections.title: What production deployment requires beyond a trained model
sections.description: Moving from a working model to production involves serving infrastructure, monitoring, version control, and integration.

content.text: Moving from a working model in development to a production deployment involves several considerations training alone doesn't address: serving infrastructure that can handle real-world request volume and latency requirements, monitoring to detect performance issues or drift after launch, version control so you can roll back if a new model version underperforms, and integration with the actual business systems that need the model's output. Teams sometimes underestimate this gap — a model that works well in testing can still fail in production due to infrastructure, integration, or scale issues entirely separate from the model's underlying accuracy.

items: Serving infrastructure — handle real-world request volume and latency.
Monitoring — detect performance issues and drift after launch.
Version control — enable rollback to previous model versions.
System integration — connect to business systems that need predictions.
Scale requirements — handle production traffic reliably.
Security and access control — protect model endpoints and data.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: A model that works in a notebook can still fail in production due to infrastructure, integration, or scale issues — deployment is its own engineering discipline, not just 'pushing code.'

Common deployment approaches include managed cloud ML platforms (AWS SageMaker, Azure AI, Google Vertex AI) that handle much of the infrastructure complexity, containerized deployment (using Docker and Kubernetes) for more control and portability across environments, and edge deployment for latency-critical or connectivity-constrained applications. The right choice depends on your team's existing infrastructure, scale requirements, and how much operational control versus managed convenience you need.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of model deployment

content.text: Model deployment has limitations and risks. Infrastructure can introduce latency and cost overhead, and scaling can be challenging without proper architecture. Deployment failures can cascade to downstream systems, and rollback complexity increases with integration depth. Monitoring gaps can lead to undetected performance degradation, and security misconfiguration can expose sensitive model endpoints. Teams can over-deploy models without proper validation, and deployment infrastructure requires ongoing maintenance.

items: Infrastructure cost — serving models adds operational expense.
Latency overhead — deployment adds network and processing delay.
Scaling challenges — high traffic requires careful architecture.
Failure cascade — deployment issues can affect downstream systems.
Rollback complexity — harder with deep system integration.
Security risk — misconfigured endpoints expose sensitive data.
Monitoring gaps — undetected performance degradation.

content.title: Important
content.text: Deployment is a bridge between data science and production engineering — neither side should own it alone. Successful deployment requires collaboration between model developers and infrastructure teams.
Deploying models effectively requires careful infrastructure planning, monitoring, and version control. The following practices can help ensure your deployment is reliable and maintainable.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Start with a staging environment that mirrors production.
Implement canary or blue-green deployments for safe rollouts.
Build comprehensive monitoring for latency, accuracy, and drift.
Implement version control with rollback capability.
Set up alerting for performance degradation and failures.
Document deployment architecture and dependencies.
Automate deployment pipelines where possible.
Plan for capacity scaling based on expected traffic.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure uptime, latency, and prediction accuracy in production. These tell you if the deployment is working — not just whether the model is accurate.

items.question: What is the difference between model deployment and model serving?
items.answer: Model deployment is the overall process of putting a model into production. Model serving is the specific runtime infrastructure that handles inference requests — deployment includes serving plus monitoring, versioning, and integration.

items.question: What is a canary deployment in model deployment?
items.answer: A canary deployment gradually introduces a new model version to a small percentage of traffic, monitoring performance before rolling out to 100%. This reduces risk and allows safe testing in production.

items.question: How do you handle A/B testing in model deployment?
items.answer: ClickMasters builds A/B testing infrastructure that routes traffic to different model versions, measuring performance differences before deciding which version to keep.

items.question: What is the difference between batch and real-time model deployment?
items.answer: Batch deployment processes predictions in bulk (e.g., overnight scoring), typically lower cost and latency-tolerant. Real-time deployment serves predictions per request (e.g., fraud detection in milliseconds), requiring lower latency and higher availability.
